newsitem.title: USA: CalEnergy launches bid for N.Y. utility.
newsitem.headline: CalEnergy launches bid for N.Y. utility.

text.p: Power company CalEnergy Co. Inc. said Tuesday it would launch a $159 million offer for 9.9 percent of New York State Electric & Gas Corp. as the first part of an attempt to buy the whole company.

CalEnergy offered to pay $24.50 per share for the stake and said it was making the move after the New York company decided not to pursue a transaction. It also said it would be willing to pay $27.50 per share for the whole company in a negotiated transaction, which would be valued at $1.9 billion based on NYSEG's 69.4 million outstanding shares.

New York State Electric's stock jumped $3.125 to $24.50 in midday trading on the New York Stock Exchange, where it was among the 20 most-active issues. CalEnergy lost 93.75 cents to $38.625, also on the NYSE.
Omaha, Neb.-based CalEnergy said it would pursue more aggressive steps if the target did not agree to a friendly transaction.
It said NYSEG had determined that a transaction was not a priority and could not be conducted on a timely basis.

However, in a letter to NYSEG Chairman Wesley von Schack, CalEnergy Chairman David Sokol said that decision appeared inconsistent with the impression left from a July 10 meeting of the two executives. He said the $27.50-per-share offer exceeded the level discussed in the meeting.

Sokol later told analysts in a conference call that the independent power producer has $2 billion in financing committed for a transaction and would pursue a proxy fight or consent solicitation if necessary.
"We at CalEnergy finish what we start," he said.
Sokol said CalEnergy already owns about 240,000 shares of NYSEG.
The tender offer, which would be conducted by CalEnergy subsidiary CE Electric Inc., calls for shareholders tendering their shares to retain the 35-cent dividend payable in August.
The proposed transaction calls for CalEnergy to maintain NYSEG as a separate operating business and keep its existing corporate headquarters in Binghamton, N.Y.

CalEnergy said it anticipated it will take nine to 12 months to complete a hostile takeover. Due to various regulatory approvals needed, that period would be shortened only slightly in the event of a friendly deal.
CalEnergy said the transaction would make NYSEG more competitive in an era of electric utility deregulation.
